Cushing’s syndrome (p.2344) can be caused by excessive secretion from an ectopic ACTH-secreting tumour. Many of these ectopic tumours express somatostatin re- ceptors and it has been suggested that octreotide may be useful in the diagnosis, and possibly the treatment, of selected patients.1 However, there are 5 types of somatostatin receptor,2,3 and re- sponses to octreotide have been variable,4 even in the same pa- tient.3,5 1. de Herder WW, Lamberts SWJ. Is there a role for somatostatin and its analogs in Cushing’s syndrome? Metabolism 1996; 45 (suppl): 83–5. 2. de Herder WW, Lamberts SWJ. Octapeptide somatostatin-ana- logue therapy of Cushing’s syndrome. Postgrad Med J 1999; 75: 65–6. 3. Uwaifo GI, et al. Is there a therapeutic role for octreotide in pa- tients with ectopic Cushing’s syndrome? J Endocrinol Invest 2003; 26: 710–17. 4. Woodhouse NJY, et al. Acute and long-term effects of octreotide in patients with ACTH-dependent Cushing’s syndrome. Am J Med 1993; 95: 305–8. 5. Gill GV, et al. Carcinoid-associated ectopic ACTH syndrome with variable response to octreotide. Postgrad Med J 1999; 75: 98–101. Diabetes mellitus. Although octreotide has been reported to impair glucose tolerance, and even precipitate frank diabetes (see Effects on Carbohydrate Metabolism, under Adverse Effects, above), its variable effects on blood glucose and insulin have led to investigations1,2 of its ability to induce beta cell rest in patients with diabetes mellitus (p.431) who still have residual insulin se- cretion.
